log.text: The sun beats down. The soil cracks.
Midsummer race: 7 run out to the stake and back, and Emser wears the oak wreath.

On midsummer night Morceem stands up by the fire and will not sit down again until Lovi and Duten come into the light. Morceem fills one bowl from the spring, puts it in Lovi's hands and then in Duten's, and they drink from it in front of everyone. More than a year of not speaking are over, and the thorn branches come off the doorsteps. From now on any quarrel on Hais is brought to the fire and ended over one shared bowl. Hais keeps the peace cup.

Midsummer on Hais: 33 people dance around a towering bonfire and feast on the best of the stores, and the ale jugs go round. Two guests from the far isle dance with them. They trade 2 hides for 300 grain. Halin of the far isle is pledged to Sane and will stay on Hais.
Timber is stacked for a new house.
The fever is back. The boat from the far isle is hardly out of sight when Serar begins to shiver.
The spring by the village runs low. The water comes up muddy and slow.

The spring is falling again. Morceem stands over it with a digging stick and says the water does not come from the stones, it comes up from under them, and will be there still when the cress goes brown. While it is low, the spring is to be dug down.
The 10th house is raised on Hais.
Sane and Halin move into a home of their own.

Morceba climbs out of the hole under the spring stones and hands the last basket of clay up to the light. At the bottom the clay is wet and cold, and the water fills it slowly from below. The sides are lined with round stones carried up from the beach, one ring laid on the next, and the shaft is knee deep below the old spring. When the summer draws the spring down now, there is water under it still. Hais has a well.
Serar died of the fever, aged 4.
The fever leaves Hais. It laid 1 islander low and took 1 of them. Morceba went from bed to bed with willow bark 3 times.
Wenar finds a wild swarm in a hollow ash and brings it home in a sack. The old log by the houses hums again.
The spring has sunk below its old stones, but the well under it still holds water. The jars go down on a rope, and nobody has to walk to the woods.
8 days of blazing heat break at last. The grain stood still in the sun.
At first light Morceem leads 9 others down to the boulders on the north-east shore with ropes of plaited hide and an armful of logs. This summer's stone is for Dorneka.
250 fields have been mucked from the heap by the pen.
Another stone goes up in the ring, raised for Dorneka: 3 of 8 stand now. 10 hands were on the ropes, and there is a feast in the ring tonight.
The sun beats down. The soil cracks.
The bucket comes up from the bottom of the well with a scrape of mud in it. Even the well under the spring is dry, knee deep, and the long walks to the pool in the woods begin again.
With the spring dry, the ale jugs come down from the rafters. The small children are given small ale with their bread, and 16 cups a day fewer have to be carried in from the pool.
The sun beats down. The soil cracks.

Wenra wades out after a cockle, steps off the edge of the sand bar and is pulled away by the sea. The other children scream from the beach. Vidor comes running, goes in to the chest, gets hold of her by the hair and drags her back, coughing and blue. Nobody goes past the knee for the rest of the summer.
Morceem and Wenar stalk the deer all morning, but a doe barks and the herd is gone into the trees.

The last sheaf on Hais is cut and carried in, and Hamor twists a handful of its straw into a little figure with arms and hangs it over the hearth. That night nobody goes to bed. 20 jugs of ale go round the fire, the old sing songs nobody has sung since they left the far shore, and the children fall asleep where they sit. From now on the end of the harvest is kept with ale: Hais has a harvest home.
Water rises in the well again after 30 dry days. The skins and jars are hung up.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the hearth smoke hangs in a flat sheet over the roofs. "Fog by morning." The goats will stay in the pen tomorrow, and the little ones by the houses.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
Vidor and Duten creep up through the long grass downwind and bring down a deer.
The rats are back. Fresh droppings in the granary, and the heap is tunnelled through.
Hamor and Wenar welcome a daughter, Servi.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the dew is down on the grass before dark. "Fog by morning." The goats will stay in the pen tomorrow, and the little ones by the houses.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
Vidor and Duten creep up through the long grass downwind and bring down a deer.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the wind has died away and the sea lies flat and oily. "Fog by morning." The goats will stay in the pen tomorrow, and the little ones by the houses.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the hearth smoke beats down and creeps along the ground. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
The storm Morceem read in the sky comes in at first light. The village is ready for it.
Two days of storms batter Hais, but the village holds. The stones on the thatch held a roof the wind tried to lift.
Vilo and Morceem welcome a son, Dorba.
After 8 days of rain a goat is limping again. The foot rot is back in the muddy pen.
A squall comes down on the deep water with Vidor out in the dugout. Half of Hais runs down to the landing to watch.
A wave comes green over the side and the dugout rolls. Vidor is in the water, a long swim from the landing.

Vidor the Hunter drowned off the landing when a squall rolled the dugout over, aged 33. In her life she took 5 wolves, 13 boars and 22 deer, landed 6,753 fish, reaped 17,755 grain, helped raise 6 roofs and hauled 3 stones up to the ring. Hais will tell of her at the fire.
For days after, pieces of the dugout wash up along the beach.
9 days of rain end. The fields have drunk deep.
The last goat is let out of the sick fold. The foot rot laid 1 goat lame; 1 hoof was pared.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the gulls are coming in off the sea in a hurry. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
The storm Morceem read in the sky comes in at first light. The village is ready for it.
A week of rain ends. The fields have drunk deep.
Five days of storms batter Hais: 1 roof torn away, 3 fences blown down.

After five days of storm Hamor walks the north-west beach to see what the sea has thrown up, and finds planks: the broken ribs and sides of a boat bigger than any dugout, pegged together by hands nobody on Hais knows. Among them, face down at the edge of the surf, lies a woman. Hamor shouts for Duten and runs. There are other shores out there than the far isle.
Hamor turns the stranger over: the sea had her long before the storm let go. Hais buries her with its own, and nobody knows what name to cut.
Nameless was found drowned among the planks of a wreck on the north-west beach, aged 23.
A storm-torn roof is mended.
Duten and Hamor track the pack to its den and kill a wolf. Its pelt will hang by the fire.
The cheese rack by the goat pen is full: 60 rounds drying on the rods. The rest of the milk is drunk.
The first snow of the winter settles on Hais. By noon the green is white and the paths are trodden black.
The planks of the wreck on the north-west beach are dragged up above the tide line: 24 timber of good split oak. Its ribs are left in the sand.
Wenra and Bamor finish a snowman by the hearth with a wolf pelt of dead bracken over its shoulders. The children call it Duten the Wolf-slayer.
Nean and Wenra finish a snowman by the hearth with a beard of dry grass. The children call it Morceem.
Six days of snow end. Drifts lie deep against the houses.
A hard frost grips the island. The woodpile shrinks fast.
Wolf prints again by the doors in the morning snow. Duten reads them and the village keeps close till dark.
4 goats are killed before winter. Meat for the smoke, hides for the doorways.

A wolf comes to the back of the goat pen in the night and finds the blackthorn heaped there. It circles and circles, and once it tries to push in. In the morning there is grey fur caught on the spines and its prints all round the pen, and not one goat is missing.
A hard frost grips the island. The woodpile shrinks fast.
2 white pups lie on the sand among the seals on the south beach. The herd is 10 now.
Duten comes up from the south beach bent under the first seal: meat for the pot, a slab of blubber for the fire, and a thick grey skin pegged out to dry.

Morceem turns the first sealskin over by the fire and thinks of Vidor in the squall of year 13. The skin is sewn up tight with sinew, all but one leg, which is blown into until the whole thing is round and hard as a drum, and tied off. It goes in the bottom of the dugout on a thong. Whoever the sea rolls out of the boat now has something to hang on to.
Six days of snow end. Drifts lie deep against the houses.
The rats are back. Fresh droppings in the granary, and the heap is tunnelled through.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the hearth smoke beats down and creeps along the ground. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
The storm Morceem read in the sky comes in at first light. The village is ready for it.
Two weeks of snow end. Drifts lie deep against the houses.
Wolf prints again by the doors in the morning snow. Duten reads them and the village keeps close till dark.
Three days of storms batter Hais, but the village holds.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the gulls are coming in off the sea in a hurry. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
The storm Morceem read in the sky comes in at first light. The village is ready for it.
A thaw. The snow goes grey and then to mud, and only the drifts in the lee of the houses are left.
A storm tide at the full moon runs up over the beach and into the hollows behind it. The cockle bed is scoured down to bare shingle. 10 driftwood is dragged up off the tide line.
Three days of storms batter Hais: 2 fences blown down.

On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells again of the autumn of the eighth year: "After two days of storm Morceem walks the south-west beach to see what the sea has thrown up, and finds a whale: a grey hill of a beast longer than any house, lying in the surf with gulls already on its back."
The fever is back. Rusaan will not eat, burns hot to the touch and cries through the night.
A wolf comes out of the dark to the goat pen and digs and scrabbles at the wattle half the night. It never gets in, but in the morning the goats will not come out of the lean-to.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the hearth smoke beats down and creeps along the ground. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
The storm Morceem read in the sky comes in at first light. The village is ready for it.
The fever leaves Hais. Rusaan is up again, and nobody was lost. Morceba went from bed to bed with willow bark 7 times.
Four days of storms batter Hais: 3 fences blown down.
A hard frost grips the island. The woodpile shrinks fast.
Nean and Isthi finish a snowman by the hearth with a wolf pelt of dead bracken over its shoulders. The children call it Duten the Wolf-slayer.
Nean and Bamor finish a snowman by the hearth with a wolf pelt of dead bracken over its shoulders. The children call it Duten the Wolf-slayer.
A hard frost grips the island. The woodpile shrinks fast.
Wolf prints again by the doors in the morning snow. Duten reads them and the village keeps close till dark.
Sane and Halin welcome a daughter, Miwen.
A thaw. The snow goes grey and then to mud, and only the drifts in the lee of the houses are left.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the dew is down on the grass before dark. "Fog by morning." The goats will stay in the pen tomorrow, and the little ones by the houses.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
Nean and Celin finish a snowman by the hearth with a wolf pelt of dead bracken over its shoulders. The children call it Duten the Wolf-slayer.
Year 13 ends: 34 people, 3 born, 3 died, 10696 grain harvested.
A dry spring. The elders fear a thin harvest.
The scarecrows turned the rooks away 71 times last year.
3 fences have rotted at the stakes over the year.
Five days of snow end. Drifts lie deep against the houses.
5 jars were broken over the year. 48 still stand in the stores.
An oak is felled above the landing beach for a new dugout.
3 blankets have worn through over the year and gone for rags. 12 still lie on the beds.
The last of the snow is gone from the hollows. The ground on Hais is bare and wet.
The last snowman by the hearth slumps into the mud. Spring has come to Hais.
Racemor opens the kiln: 4 of 8 jars come out whole, 4 cracked in the fire.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the sea is warm and the air above it cold and still. "Fog by morning." The goats will stay in the pen tomorrow, and the little ones by the houses.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
A new dugout is rolled down the sand and floats. Hais can fish the deep water again.
After four days of rain a goat is limping again. The foot rot is back in the muddy pen.
A boar shoulders through a fence and roots through 1 field in the night.
In the morning a rainbow stands over the west of Hais, after six days of rain.
Olta reaches the place where the rainbow came down and stands in the wet grass and looks up, and cannot see it at all from there.
Racemor opens the kiln: 6 of 8 jars come out whole, 2 cracked in the fire.
The last goat is let out of the sick fold. The foot rot laid 1 goat lame; 1 hoof was pared.
Rusaan passed away, aged 1.
Cubs yip somewhere in the deep woods. The pack has grown.
Striped piglets trot after the sows at the forest edge.
2 fawns stand trembling in the long grass beside the does.
4 kids are born in the goat pen and are soon butting heads.

At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the far isle stands up sharp and close, every tree on it plain. "Fog by morning." The goats will stay in the pen tomorrow, and the little ones by the houses.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
The cheese rack by the goat pen is full: 60 rounds drying on the rods. The rest of the milk is drunk.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: a ring stands round the sun as it goes down. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
Morceem called a storm, but the morning comes in grey and drizzling. The children laugh at the stones hanging off the roofs.
The goats are moulting. Goan combs the loose winter coats out of the herd with a bone comb: 21 handfuls of hair for the spindles.
Duten and Hamor spear a boar in its wallow and carry it home.
A boar shoulders through a fence and roots through 1 field in the night.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the gulls are coming in off the sea in a hurry. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
The storm Morceem read in the sky comes in at first light. The village is ready for it.
Three days of storms batter Hais: 3 fields flattened, 1 roof torn away, 1 fence blown down.
A storm-torn roof is mended.
Late in the afternoon a rainbow stands over the east of Hais, after three days of rain.
Wenra reaches the place where the rainbow came down and stands in the wet grass and looks up, and cannot see it at all from there.
Duten and Hamor spear a boar in its wallow and carry it home.
In the morning a rainbow stands over the west of Hais, after three days of rain.
Isthi reaches the place where the rainbow came down and comes back soaked to the knees, sure it was just past the next field.
The rooks walk the rows right up to Morceba's scarecrow now, and one is pulling straw out of its sleeve. It will have to be moved.
A hive swarms. Wenar shakes the clump off a branch into an empty log. 2 hives in the bee garden now.
Emser's old dog Grim lies down by the hearth one evening and does not get up.
8 days of rain end. The fields have drunk deep.
In the morning a rainbow stands over the west of Hais, after 8 days of rain.
Wenfen reaches the place where the rainbow came down and stands in the wet grass and looks up, and cannot see it at all from there.
In the morning a rainbow stands over the west of Hais, after four days of rain.
The sun beats down. The soil cracks.
Olta reaches the place where the rainbow came down and finds that it has moved on, further out over the sea.
The rats are back. Fresh droppings in the granary, and the heap is tunnelled through.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
The sun beats down. The soil cracks.
The sun beats down. The soil cracks.
Rain on midsummer day. The bonfire is put off until the sky clears.
In the morning a rainbow stands over the west of Hais, after three days of rain.
Isthi reaches the place where the rainbow came down and stands in the wet grass and looks up, and cannot see it at all from there.
Midsummer race: 8 run out to the stake and back, and Anfen wears the oak wreath.

Anfen slaps the hazel stake and is back at the bonfire first for the third midsummer, and the oak wreath goes on his head before he has caught his breath. From now on the children call him Anfen the Swift, and race each other along the paths to be next.
After 3 days of waiting for the sky to clear, midsummer on Hais: 33 people dance around a towering bonfire and feast on the best of the stores, and the ale jugs go round.
At first light Morceem leads 9 others down to the boulders on the north-east shore with ropes of plaited hide and an armful of logs. This summer's stone is for Katen.
Harvest home: the last sheaf is in and a new straw figure hangs over the hearth. 20 jugs of ale go round, and the singing goes on until nearly midnight.
The sun beats down. The soil cracks.
Another stone goes up in the ring, raised for Katen: 4 of 8 stand now. 10 hands were on the ropes, and there is a feast in the ring tonight.
The spring by the village runs low. The water comes up muddy and slow.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the hearth smoke beats down and creeps along the ground. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
The storm Morceem read in the sky comes in at first light. The village is ready for it.
The great clawed prints are in the sand below the tide line again, coming in off the bar. Broad-Back is back for the honey, and the children are kept by the houses after dark.

By evening the hurdle is off the bear pit. Duten drives sharpened stakes into its floor, and hazel rods and turf go over the top until it looks like the grass around it. The children are told where it is, and told again.
Morceba and Lovi welcome a daughter, Baru.
Four days of storms batter Hais, but the village holds.
The sun beats down. The soil cracks.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the dew is down on the grass before dark. "Fog by morning." The goats will stay in the pen tomorrow, and the little ones by the houses.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
The sun beats down. The soil cracks.
The spring by the village runs low. The water comes up muddy and slow.
Duten and Hamor stalk the deer all morning, but a doe barks and the herd is gone into the trees.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: a long swell rolls in under a sea as flat as a plate. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
The storm Morceem read in the sky comes in at first light. The village is ready for it.
In the morning the prints of Broad-Back come down from the trees to the edge of the bear pit, stop, and go round it. A clawed hole is torn in the turf at one corner where it smelled the fresh earth.

In the dead of night Cull starts up barking at the bee logs and will not stop. Hamor runs out with a burning brand and finds Broad-Back up on its hind legs with its head in a log, eating the comb. She shouts and swings the brand, and the bear drops down and lumbers off into the trees, swatting at the bees.
Three days of storms batter Hais: 1 roof torn away, 2 fences blown down.
A storm-torn roof is mended.
Duten and Emser creep up through the long grass downwind and bring down a deer.

In the dead of night Cull starts up barking at the bee logs and will not stop. Hamor runs out with a burning brand and finds Broad-Back up on its hind legs with its head in a log, eating the comb. She shouts and swings the brand, and the bear drops down and lumbers off into the trees, swatting at the bees.
Duten and Hamor creep up through the long grass downwind and bring down a deer.
At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the hearth smoke hangs in a flat sheet over the roofs. "Fog by morning." The goats will stay in the pen tomorrow, and the little ones by the houses.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
Miwen passed away, aged 0.
A squall comes down on the deep water with Duten out in the dugout. Half of Hais runs down to the landing to watch.
Duten comes in through the surf half swamped, bailing with both hands. The catch went over the side to keep the dugout up, all but 2 fish.

At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the sky in the west is red as an ember and mares' tails stand high up. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
The storm Morceem read in the sky comes in at first light. The village is ready for it.
A week of storms batters Hais: 1 roof torn away.
Fog rolls in off the sea. The shore goes quiet and the trees fade to grey.
A storm-torn roof is mended.

At the evening fire Morceem looks out to sea: the sky in the west is red as an ember and mares' tails stand high up. "A storm by morning." The ripe grain is cut by firelight and stones are hung on the thatch.
Morceem called a storm, but the morning comes in grey and drizzling. The children laugh at the stones hanging off the roofs.

In the dead of night Cull starts up barking at the bee logs and will not stop. Hamor runs out with a burning brand and finds Broad-Back up on its hind legs with its head in a log, eating the comb. She shouts and swings the brand, and the bear drops down and lumbers off into the trees, swatting at the bees.

chronicle.text: 8 settlers land on Hais and light a fire.
Vidor wades into the shallows with a sharpened stick and comes back with fish. Hais learns to fish.
Saaris lays a timber floor on four posts and heaps the grain on it, out of the damp. Hais learns to build granaries.
The first granary stands on Hais, its floor raised above the damp.
Saaris watches the clouds pile up over the sea and says the gentle days are over. From now on the sky brings rain, storms, heat and hard frost.
Saaris finds great paw prints in the mud and hears howling from the deep woods. Wolves live on Hais, and boars root among the trees.
Saaris lashes a flint point to a long ash pole. If the beasts come for Hais, Hais will go out after them. The islanders learn to hunt.
Boars root through 3 fields by the woods in the night. The grain is trampled and torn up. Nobody on Hais has an answer for them yet.
Vidor and Duten spear a boar in its wallow and carry it home. The first boar taken on Hais; there is roast pork at the fire tonight.
Saaris says the longest day should not pass like any other. On midsummer evening the work will stop, the fire will be built high, and all of Hais will dance around it.
At first light Saaris sees four deer grazing on the open grass east of the village. They lift their heads, stare, and are gone into the trees. Not everything in the woods of Hais has teeth.
Midsummer on Hais: 9 people dance around a towering bonfire and feast on the best of the stores. The first midsummer fire on Hais burns until nearly midnight.
Saaris drives a row of stakes along the trampled grain and weaves hazel rods between them. Hais learns to fence its fields.
Racemor ties off the last hazel rod. The first fence on Hais stands between the grain and the woods.
Boars snuffle along the new fences all night and find no way in. In the morning the grain stands untouched.

A wall of grey rolls in off the sea and swallows Hais. From the beach Saaris cannot see the water, and from the fields nobody can see the trees. Nobody fishes and nobody hunts, and somewhere out in the white a wolf howls in broad day.
Vidor and Duten creep up through the long grass downwind and bring down a deer. The first venison on Hais; the hide is pegged out to dry and the bones are kept for needles.
A wolf leaps on Vidor out of the fog. She limps home, badly bitten. For weeks after, nobody stays out past dusk.
The grass between the hearth and the beach is trodden down to bare earth. Nobody laid it out; the feet of Hais did. Saaris notices the walk is quicker on it, and the others follow the track.
Vidor and Duten track the pack to its den and kill a wolf. Its pelt will hang by the fire. The first wolf ever slain on Hais.

Saaris walks out to a quiet patch of ground north of the village and sets a ring of stones there. Arys is laid in the earth inside it, and 3 mourners stand at the graveside next morning. Hais has a burying ground.
Hais is home to 10 people.
Wenra, the first child born on Hais, arrives to Seran and Morceem.
Wolves take Saaris in the fog. Nobody saw them come. Hais learns to fear the dark woods. For weeks after, nobody stays out past dusk.
Four days of fog lift. Out of the grey, wolves took one of the village.

The wolves come out of the fog, and nobody hears them until it is too late. Morceem brings up a great whelk shell from the beach, knocks off its tip and blows: a low moan rolls out over the fields and into the trees. On fog days now someone keeps by the hearth and blows the horn, and whoever can hear it can call back. Hais has a fog horn.

A raft of lashed logs drifts onto the beach with nobody aboard but three goats, thin and bleating. Morceem wades out and leads them ashore, and by nightfall a wattle pen stands beside the village. Morceem takes a crook and goes out with them each morning. Hais keeps goats.

Hamor comes in from the edge of the woods with a wolf cub in her arms, thin and shivering; it had crept out of the den alone. The grown-ups argue half the night about knocking it on the head. In the end it stays: Hamor calls him Cull, feeds him fish heads and lets him sleep across the doorway. Cull grows up thinking the village is his pack. Hais has a dog.

Something has been at the grain: husks strewn over the granary floor, droppings in the chaff, a little trail worn into the grass. At dusk Morceem sees a grey shape run along the granary beam and drop into the heap. Rats have come to Hais, and nobody knows how they came ashore.

On midsummer day Morceem sees a dugout come in over the sea with 3 strangers at the paddles. They come from an isle beyond the haze, where the midsummer fires of Hais have been seen. Their words are strange, but they have come for the dance. Hais is not alone in the sea.
A week of storms batters Hais: 1 roof torn away, 2 fences blown down.

The rats have multiplied past counting. At night the granary floor seethes, they run along the rafters and squeal in the thatch, and Emser wakes screaming with one on the blanket. Whatever grain they do not eat, they foul.

A wolf tears through the back of the goat pen in the night and drags off a kid. Nobody wakes until it is over; in the morning there is a hole in the wattle and a red trail across the snow. The winter woods are empty, and the wolves have found the goat pen.

The nights are long and black, and Morceem, the eldest, says the old days must not be forgotten. On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells of the fog: how it comes in off the sea without a sound, how a child who strays past the last house cannot find the way back, and how the wolves walk in it by day. Saaris went out into it and did not come home. Nobody fidgets. Since that night the children of Hais keep close to the houses when the fog comes in. From now on a tale is told every year on the longest night.
Vidor carries home her tenth kill. The children play at being Vidor the Hunter now, with sticks for spears.
A fever comes to Hais. The boat from the far isle is hardly out of sight when Racemor begins to shiver. Nobody on Hais has seen its like, and nobody knows what to do but keep the fire going and wait.

After Katen is laid in the earth, Seran walks to the edge of the woods and comes back with willow bark and bitter leaves. She steeps them by the fire and spoons the brew into the sick. Hais learns the herb lore, and has a healer.
The fever leaves Hais. It laid 3 islanders low and took 1 of them. Seran went from bed to bed with willow bark 9 times.

In the grey of the morning Racemor finds the granary door hanging open and the floor swept half bare: 280 grain are gone. Down on the beach there are footprints and the long groove of a keel, and only the far isle has a boat. The far isle has had a thin year, and its people have not forgotten the granaries they saw at midsummer. Next summer nobody on Hais will look for their boat.
Duten pegs out a third wolf pelt beside the others. Around the fire they have started calling him Duten the Wolf-slayer, and the children hush when he walks by.

On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells of the landing: how 8 people came over the sea in the first spring with seed grain, stone axes and a pot of embers, and lit the fire they are sitting round.

On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Seran tells again of the winter of the first year: "Saaris walks out to a quiet patch of ground north of the village and sets a ring of stones there."

Sick of sweeping rat droppings out of the grain, Racemor digs sticky grey clay from the bank above the beach, rolls it into ropes and coils them into a jar with a fat belly and a narrow neck. She heaps turf and clay into a dome beside the village to fire it in. Grain sealed in a jar under a clay lid is out of the rats' reach. Hais learns to make pots.

Racemor rakes the embers off the kiln and lifts out the first jars, still warm: 6 of 8 come out whole and ring like stone when tapped. The grain is poured in and the lids are sealed with wet clay. For the first time the rats run over the jars and cannot get in.

Twice now raiders from the far isle have come for the granary in the night. Morceem walks down to the beach where their dugout ran ashore, piles up driftwood above the tide line and says that from now on, from the harvest to midwinter, somebody will sit up there by a fire and watch the sea. Hais keeps a beach watch.

Lovi sits up by the beach fire under a moon as round as a jar lid, after 72 nights of watching, and the sea lies bright and empty all the way to the far isle. Counting back on his fingers, he sees it: both boats came in the dark of the moon, or under a fog. Lovi cuts a notch in the granary doorpost for this night and says they will cut one for every night after, and light the beach fire only when the moon is thin. Hais learns to count the moon.

The snow lies knee-deep and the houses are full of smoke and squabbling, so the children are sent out to the green. Emser and Wenra pack a snowball, roll it until it will not move, and heave a second one on top. By dusk a white figure stands by the hearth with pebble eyes and a stick for a nose, and the children of Hais build snowmen every winter from now on.
On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells of his own young days: he landed 114 fish and reaped 2,236 grain. His hands show it as he talks.

After three days of rain the clouds tear open. Late in the afternoon the sun comes out low and a great bow of colours stands over the east of Hais, its feet in the wet grass. Nobody has a word for it. Wenra runs off to find where it comes down, and the other children run after.

Vidor has stood on the beach two summers now and watched the far isle's dugout come in over the swell. This spring she fells a tall straight oak above the landing, lights small fires along its back and scrapes out the charcoal with a shell, a little every dry day. She means to fish where the big ones are, out past the surf. Hais learns to hollow a dugout.

Emys comes in from the woodpile white in the face. A wolf stood at the edge of the trees at midday and watched him, alone and bold as a dog, with one eye milky and blind. The spears have kept the pack at the den small for years, and a young wolf driven out of it has nowhere to go but here. It walks by day, when the others sleep. The islanders call it Pale-Eye.

Vidor and a crowd of helpers roll the hollowed oak down the sand on logs and push it out into the surf. It wallows, rights itself and floats. Hais has a boat of its own, and the deep water past the breakers is no longer out of reach.

Out at the edge of the woods Morceem stops by a hazel he cut down two winters ago. The stump has not died: a ring of straight green poles has sprung up from it, taller than a child. He says a tree cut low grows back faster than a seedling ever could, and that the stumps nearest the village must be left in the ground and fenced from the goats. That day 6 trees are cut to the stool. Hais learns to coppice.

Racemor straightens up from the sheaves and looks back along the rows. The grain on the side by the goat pen, where the dung has been forked out over the wattle for years, stands a head taller than the rest, the ears fat and heavy. She says the muck should not be wasted on a corner. From now on it goes on a heap by the pen with the hearth ash and the scraps, and after the harvest it is carried out in baskets and forked over the bare fields. Hais learns to muck its fields.

Duten and Hamor come on Pale-Eye asleep in the bracken after 4 hunts, and put a spear through it before it is up. The pelt, paler and bigger than any from the den, is pegged out by the hearth, and that night everybody stays up late round the fire.

Duten scrapes the pelt of Pale-Eye clean, rubs it soft with ash and works it for days by the fire, then throws it over his shoulders, the head hanging down his back. He wears it everywhere now. The wolves at the treeline smell one of their own on him and keep away. Hais learns to make a wolf-skin cloak.
Vidor comes in through the surf in the dugout with 12 fish in the bottom of it, fat ones the size of a forearm that never come near the beach. The children run down the sand to see.

The wind drops and Morceem climbs up to look at the torn thatch. Morceem has sat out 130 days of storm on Hais, and says every one of them was told the evening before, for anyone who could read it: a red sky in the west, mares' tails high up, the gulls coming in off the sea, the hearth smoke beating down. From now on, at the evening fire, the eldest will look out over the sea and say what the morning will bring. Hais learns to read the sky.

A ragged black cloud comes up out of the woods at first light, wheels once over the houses, calling, and drops onto the ripe grain. Rooks: 8 of them, walking the rows like old men, pulling the ears down and stripping them. Morceem runs at them waving both arms and they lift, but they only settle again further down the rows. There is enough grain on Hais now for the rooks to think it worth the flight.

Racemor is splitting a dead oak at the edge of the woods when the axe goes into a hollow and the whole trunk starts to hum. She runs, stung on the neck and the hands. That evening she comes back with a smoking brand, saws the hollow length off above and below, plugs the ends with turf and rolls it home with the bees still inside. The log is stood on end beside the village with a flat stone on top, and by morning the bees are going in and out of the split as if nothing had happened. Hais keeps bees.

Morceem watches the guests at the midsummer fire: sharp cheekbones, no hides, nothing to trade. Morceem remembers the open granary door of year 6 and says it is better to give the grain by day than lose it by night. Hais learns to send hungry guests home with a gift.

The heat lies on Hais like a blanket and the children are good for nothing, so Emser leads them down to the beach below the village. They wade in to the knee and shriek at the cold, and Nean feels something hard under a toe: a cockle. By evening they come home wet through with their shirts full of shells, and from now on the children go down to the shallows on hot afternoons.

Black clouds roll in off the sea at first light, just as Morceem said they would. This time the ripe grain is already in and the roofs are roped down with stones, and everyone is indoors before the first gust. Nobody on Hais laughs at sky-reading now.

Morceem lifts the stone off the bee log, wafts in smoke from a smouldering brand and cuts out the heavy comb from the top, leaving the bottom for the bees to winter on. The comb is squeezed through a cloth into a clay jar: 6 measures of dark honey. The children lick the cloth clean.

Emser takes the morning milk out to the grazing in a bag sewn from the stomach of a kid killed last autumn, and leaves it hanging on a thorn in the sun. By noon it has gone to soft white curd in thin green whey. Morceem tastes it and does not spit it out. The curd is tipped into a wicker basket with a flat stone on top, the whey runs out through the weave, and in a few days there is a firm pale round with a rind on it. A rack of hazel rods goes up against the pen wall, out of the rain, to dry the rounds. Half the summer milk goes to the press now, to be eaten when the frost comes. Hais learns to make cheese.

Four days of fog lift, and Morceem sits on by the evening fire long after the others have gone in. On Hais wolves have come out of it 3 times and Saaris did not come home from it. Thinking back over every grey morning, he finds the sign was always there the night before: the wind dropping away, the sea lying flat and oily, the far isle standing up sharp and close, the dew down early on the grass. From now on, when the eldest says "fog by morning", the goats stay in the pen and the small ones by the houses. Hais learns the fog signs.

Out on the deep water Vidor looks up from the line. The sky over the sea has gone black in the time it takes to haul a fish, and a wall of rain is walking across the water toward the dugout. On the beach the shore fishers shout and point, and soon all of Hais is running down to the landing to watch her fight the paddle home. Nobody knew the weather out there could turn so fast.

After two days of storm Morceem walks the south-west beach to see what the sea has thrown up, and finds a whale: a grey hill of a beast longer than any house, lying in the surf with gulls already on its back. It is dead. By noon every islander who can carry a knife is down there, cutting. Hais learns that the sea sometimes gives as well as takes.

The frost bites hard and the smoke hangs low over the roofs. 1 round comes down off the rack by the goat pen and is cut into wedges by the fire, one for each of the little ones and the old. The summer milk has kept, and it keeps them going. 4 rounds are left on the rack.
Grey fog lies over Hais at first light, just as Morceem said it would. The pen gate stays shut and the children are kept in. Out in the white a wolf howls, and finds nothing to take.

On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells again of the autumn of the first year: "Vidor and Duten creep up through the long grass downwind and bring down a deer."

Five times since the fences went up a boar has shouldered through the wattle, and Morceem is tired of mending it. He walks along the wood's edge and points at the thickets of hawthorn there: not one boar track goes through them. This autumn, he says, slips of thorn will be dug from the woods and set along every field by the trees. For three summers they will be nothing but twigs, but then they will be a wall no boar can push through, and a hedge does not rot. Hais learns to plant hedges.

The sowing is done and the shoots are up when the cold comes back. For six days the nights are clear and still, and every dawn the fields are white. When it lifts, Morceem walks the rows and pulls up a handful of black, limp stalks: the frost has killed the young grain in 2 fields. On 29 more fields the leaf tips are burnt brown. There is nothing for it but to dig them over and sow again, and hope the seed is quicker than the summer. Nobody on Hais had thought the spring could turn.

Morceem counts the bare patches in the rows and says the grown-ups cannot stand in the fields all day. That evening two flat boards are tied loosely together with a thong, and Emser is shown how to swing them so they clap like a branch breaking. From now on, when the rooks come down, the children run out with clappers and stones and shout until they lift. Hais keeps bird-scarers.

After five days of warm rain, Morceem pulls a stalk from a field of young grain and holds it up: the leaves are flecked with orange, like a blade left out in the wet, and the dust of it comes off on the fingers. Nobody on Hais has seen it before. Nobody knows that the wind and the rain will carry it to the fields beside it.
With Seran gone, Morceba takes down the herb basket from its peg. Hais has its second healer.

Last summer's honey has stood all year in a sealed jar with water from the spring, and it has turned. Racemor lifts the lid at midsummer and the smell fills the hearth: sweet, sharp and strong. A bowl goes from hand to hand round the bonfire, and the dancing gets louder and later than it has ever been. Hais has mead.

Hamor comes back from the woods with a basket of thorny slips and torn hands, and heels them into a trench along the field by the trees, a hand apart. They look like nothing at all. The first hedge is planted on Hais.

After four days of rain the goat pen is a wallow of mud and dung, churned knee-deep by the gate. Emser finds one of the goats holding up a foreleg and hobbling on three; between the claws the hoof is soft, grey and stinking. The lame ones lie down in the straw and will not go out to graze, and their milk dries up. Nobody on Hais has seen it before, and nobody knows what to do for it but wait for the ground to dry.
The pen dries out and the last lame goat walks sound again. The foot rot laid 17 goats lame and killed 2.

Morceba has buried 2 goats that the foot rot took, and has watched the rest. The lame ones that limped up onto the dry bank mended; the ones left lying in the mud gave it to the others. Morceba weaves hurdles into a little fold against the pen wall and lays it with dry straw. Next time a goat limps it will be caught, the rotten horn pared back to clean hoof with a flint, the foot washed in willow-bark brew, and the goat put in the fold until it walks sound. Hais learns to pare hooves.

On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells how Vidor came to be called Vidor the Hunter: she took 4 wolves, 7 boars and 15 deer, landed 3,504 fish, reaped 10,081 grain and helped raise 4 roofs. Vidor looks into the fire and says nothing.

Vidor catches the limping goat by the horns, sits on it in the straw and pares the soft grey horn away with a flint until the hoof shows pink and clean. The foot is washed in willow-bark brew, the goat is lifted over the hurdles into the dry fold, and it stands there on three legs, bleating at the others. The first hoof is pared on Hais.
The last goat is let out of the sick fold. The foot rot laid 1 goat lame; 1 hoof was pared. Morceba was right: caught early and kept out of the mud, it went no further.
Hais is home to 25 people.

On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells how Duten came to be called Duten the Wolf-slayer: he took 5 wolves, 8 boars and 17 deer, landed 2,176 fish, reaped 8,379 grain and helped raise 2 roofs. Duten looks into the fire and says nothing.

The children have run out after the rooks 40 times, and still the flock comes back. Morceem watches it come in over the trees and turn away from a field where somebody stands hoeing, and laughs: they are afraid of a man, not of a clapper. That evening two poles are lashed into a cross and stuffed with straw, an old hide is hung over the arms, and the figure is carried out to the fields. Hais learns to make scarecrows.

Duten drives the poles into the middle of a field and hangs an old hide on the arms. In the wind it flaps and turns, and from the trees it looks like someone standing there. The first scarecrow stands on Hais.

A roar goes up from the bee log and a cloud of bees pours out into the sun, whirls over the houses and settles in a hanging clump on a hazel bough. Racemor holds a fresh hollow log under it and gives the bough one hard shake. Most of the bees fall in, and the rest follow them by dusk. Hais has two hives.

For days now round dark heads have come up in the swell behind the dugout, watching with big wet eyes, and sinking without a ripple when anyone looks back. This evening Vidor walks the south beach and finds them: 5 grey seals hauled up on the sand, fat as sacks of grain, groaning to each other. They have followed the fish in. Hais has seals.

All summer the children of Hais have been racing each other down to the beach and back. On midsummer evening Morceem drives a hazel stake into the grass out past the bonfire and says that whoever slaps it and is back at the fire first will wear the oak wreath. 4 line up, the whole village shouts, and Anfen, 21, comes in first. From now on the young run at every midsummer.

Morceem stands a long time by the burying ground, where the ring of small stones round the dead is half grown over with grass. The stores are fuller than they have ever been, he says, the grain is in and there are hands to spare: Hais should raise something that will still be standing when everyone at the fire tonight is in the ground. On the open grass east of the village he walks a circle round a peg on a cord and drives in eight stakes. Down on the north-east shore lie grey boulders as long as a man. He says one will be dragged up on rollers every summer after the harvest, and stood in the ring for one of the dead. Hais begins a ring of standing stones.

Lovi comes up from the beach at first light white in the face. In the wet sand below the tide line there are prints as long as a forearm, five claws pressed deep in front of each, coming in off the bar from the far isle and going straight up into the woods. At dusk something big breaks through the bracken at the edge of the trees, stands up on its hind legs to sniff the wind, and drops down again: a bear, with shoulders as wide as a doorway. Nobody alive on Hais has ever seen one. It has smelled the honey from across the water. The islanders call it Broad-Back.

10 islanders lean back on the ropes, the stone tips over the lip of the pit and drops in with a thud the children feel through their feet. Packed round with rubble and stamped down, it stands taller than any of them: the first standing stone on Hais, raised for Arys. That night the stores are opened and there is a feast in the ring.

In the dead of night Cull starts up barking at the bee logs and will not stop. Hamor runs out with a burning brand and finds Broad-Back up on its hind legs with its head in a log, eating the comb. She shouts and swings the brand, and the bear drops down and lumbers off into the trees, swatting at the bees. Before it goes it turns and swipes once, and Hamor is carried home with her shoulder torn open. Nobody on Hais sleeps soundly after that.

In the dark before dawn Olta wakes coughing: a hard dry cough that comes in long fits until she cannot get a breath, and then a great whooping gasp as the air goes back in. The grown-ups look at each other over her head. Every one of the settlers had this as a child, far away over the sea, and remembers it; none of the 15 children born on Hais ever has. Nobody knows anything to do for it but keep the little ones warm and sit up with them through the night.

The log by the houses has gone quiet. When the stone is lifted the comb is empty and the bees lie in a dry heap at the bottom. The winter was too long for the comb they had. From now on more comb is left in the logs at the honey taking. There are no bees left on Hais but the wild ones in the woods.

The first frost is white on the grass, and the prints of Broad-Back go down onto the sand at low tide and out along the bar towards the far isle. Broad-Back came into the village on 14 nights and took 54 comb from the logs and 30 rounds of cheese off the rack, and split 1 log open; it was driven off with brands 9 times. The split log is stood up again and bound with withies for a swarm next spring. It will remember the way.
The whooping cough leaves Hais. 16 islanders coughed through it, and every one of them is still here.

On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells of Arys, who died of the cold in the first year. The little ones ask where the mound is, and are told.

Lovi climbs out of the pit by the bee logs on a notched pole and pulls it up after him. It is deeper than a man is tall, the sides cut sheer, the spoil carried off into the trees so nothing shows. A wattle hurdle is laid over it for now. When the clawed prints come in off the bar again, stakes will go into its floor and turf over the top. Let Broad-Back come for the comb again. Hais has a bear pit.

Lovi and Duten fall out over where one woodpile ends and the other begins, and then over everything else. From that day Lovi's house and Duten's house do not speak. A thorn branch is laid across each doorstep, nobody from one will sit by anyone from the other at the fire, and no child of one will be married to a child of the other. It is the first feud on Hais, and nobody knows how to end it.

In the grey of the morning the first one down to the spring with a skin comes back with it empty. Between the stones there is only a skin of cracked mud, and the cress on the bank has gone brown. Nobody on Hais has seen it fail before. Morceem remembers a deep pool in the woods where the deer go to drink, a long walk under the trees, and by noon a line of islanders is going out to it with skins and jars and coming back bent under the weight. Until the rain comes, every cup on Hais is carried in from the woods.

Morceem watches Emser carry a full skin of water up from the spring without stopping, and says he has seen him grow a hand taller since the spring. But nobody on Hais should become grown just by getting tall. Tonight the moon is full, and Emser will walk out to the standing stones, sit alone till first light by the stone raised for Arys, with a small fire and his back to the village, and walk home at dawn. His mother packs his cloak with a heel of bread. From now on every child of Hais sits a night at the stones in the first autumn after turning thirteen.
At first light Emser walks home from the standing stones, stiff with cold and grey with ash, and Morceem hands him the first bowl at the hearth. Emser is counted among the grown now.

The rain has got in under the lid of a jar of the new grain, and when Racemor tips it out the seed has sprouted, a pale beard on every grain. She cannot bear to throw it to the goats, so she dries it on a hide by the fire, cracks it on a flat stone and steeps it in a pot of hot water. It turns sweet as honey. Three days later the pot is frothing and sour-smelling, and the first cup of it goes round the hearth to a great deal of coughing and laughing. Hamor hollows out a log for a vat and sets it against the wall of her house. Hais learns to brew ale.

The frost has the island by the throat and the children cry with the cold at night. Morceem walks round the goat pen and pulls the tufts of moulted hair off the wattle, a whole fistful of it, and sits by the fire twisting it between finger and thumb into a thread. He hangs a stone off the end and sets it spinning, and the thread draws itself out long and even. He lashes two poles against the wall of his house with a beam across the top, hangs the threads from it in a row and ties clay weights from the kiln on the ends to pull them straight. Thread goes over and under, and a hand's breadth of rough grey cloth grows on the frame. Hais learns to spin and weave.

Vidor has watched the seals take 576 fish out of the deep water in front of the dugout, and the catch grow thin. Now there are pups on the sand, white as snow, and the herd is 8. She cuts a short club of blackthorn and walks out to the south beach at low tide, keeping between the seals and the sea. From now on, when the pups are on the sand, the hunters go down to the seals: meat for the pot, blubber for the fires, and skins for whatever the dugout needs. Hais learns to take seals.

Morceem cuts the first blanket down off the loom: goat hair, grey and brown, rough as a dog's back and as warm. It goes on the bed where the youngest sleep. Nobody on Hais has slept under cloth before.

The snow stopped before dawn. Duten is first out of doors and finds Hais written over in the night: the paired slots of deer along the meadow edge and the round four-toed pads of wolves in a line out of the trees and right up to the doors. He follows one line until the prints are so fresh the snow is still crumbling at their edges. Hais learns to read tracks in the snow.

On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells of Saaris, who was dragged down by wolves in the fog in the second year. The little ones ask where the mound is, and are told.

8 goats have gone out through the back of the pen in the night, and every time the hole is in the same place, the side away from the houses. Morceem stands looking at it with a torn hand from the hawthorn. The thorn keeps the boars out of the grain, he says; let thorn keep the wolves out of the goats. He cuts a great armful of blackthorn at the wood's edge, drags it back by the butts and heaps it against the wattle, spines outward. No wolf will put its face into that. Hais builds a thorn fold.

A wolf comes to the back of the goat pen in the night and finds the blackthorn heaped there. It circles and circles, and once it tries to push in. In the morning there is grey fur caught on the spines and a ring of prints trodden round the pen in the snow, and not one goat is missing. The thorn fold has turned its first wolf.

A boar comes snuffling out of the trees in the night and walks the length of the hawthorn, looking for a way through. There is none. In the morning there are tufts of bristle caught on the thorns and the grain behind them stands untouched. The hedges have grown.

In broad day a dugout comes in over the sea from the far isle, low in the water with bundles and a pot of embers, and 3 people climb out onto the sand: Sane with 2 children. They have not come for a dance. Sane's man was lost at sea in the autumn, and the house she was left in is not hers. Morceem walks down to meet them, looks back at the full granaries and the empty ground beyond the fields, and says there is room on Hais. They sleep where there is space until a house is raised for them. For the first time since the landing, Hais has taken in new people.

On day 2 of the storm, with the full moon pulling the tide high, the sea does not stop at the sand. It comes up over the beach, into the hollows behind the dunes and far up the low ground in a sheet of grey water, and by evening it has drained back and left a long line of weed and 6 armfuls of driftwood. No field lay low enough to drown. Morceem looks from the tide line up to the fields and says grain must never be sown down there. The dugout is lifted off the landing and thrown up into the dunes, split from end to end. The cockle bed is scoured down to bare shingle. Hais learns what a storm tide can do.

On midsummer night Morceem stands up by the fire and will not sit down again until Lovi and Duten come into the light. Morceem fills one bowl from the spring, puts it in Lovi's hands and then in Duten's, and they drink from it in front of everyone. More than a year of not speaking are over, and the thorn branches come off the doorsteps. From now on any quarrel on Hais is brought to the fire and ended over one shared bowl. Hais keeps the peace cup.
The 10th house is raised on Hais.

Morceba climbs out of the hole under the spring stones and hands the last basket of clay up to the light. At the bottom the clay is wet and cold, and the water fills it slowly from below. The sides are lined with round stones carried up from the beach, one ring laid on the next, and the shaft is knee deep below the old spring. When the summer draws the spring down now, there is water under it still. Hais has a well.

Wenra wades out after a cockle, steps off the edge of the sand bar and is pulled away by the sea. The other children scream from the beach. Vidor comes running, goes in to the chest, gets hold of her by the hair and drags her back, coughing and blue. Nobody goes past the knee for the rest of the summer.

The last sheaf on Hais is cut and carried in, and Hamor twists a handful of its straw into a little figure with arms and hangs it over the hearth. That night nobody goes to bed. 20 jugs of ale go round the fire, the old sing songs nobody has sung since they left the far shore, and the children fall asleep where they sit. From now on the end of the harvest is kept with ale: Hais has a harvest home.

Vidor the Hunter drowned off the landing when a squall rolled the dugout over, aged 33. In her life she took 5 wolves, 13 boars and 22 deer, landed 6,753 fish, reaped 17,755 grain, helped raise 6 roofs and hauled 3 stones up to the ring. Hais will tell of her at the fire.

After five days of storm Hamor walks the north-west beach to see what the sea has thrown up, and finds planks: the broken ribs and sides of a boat bigger than any dugout, pegged together by hands nobody on Hais knows. Among them, face down at the edge of the surf, lies a woman. Hamor shouts for Duten and runs. There are other shores out there than the far isle.

Morceem turns the first sealskin over by the fire and thinks of Vidor in the squall of year 13. The skin is sewn up tight with sinew, all but one leg, which is blown into until the whole thing is round and hard as a drum, and tied off. It goes in the bottom of the dugout on a thong. Whoever the sea rolls out of the boat now has something to hang on to.

On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells again of the autumn of the eighth year: "After two days of storm Morceem walks the south-west beach to see what the sea has thrown up, and finds a whale: a grey hill of a beast longer than any house, lying in the surf with gulls already on its back."

Anfen slaps the hazel stake and is back at the bonfire first for the third midsummer, and the oak wreath goes on his head before he has caught his breath. From now on the children call him Anfen the Swift, and race each other along the paths to be next.
The great clawed prints are in the sand below the tide line again, coming in off the bar. Broad-Back is back for the honey, and the children are kept by the houses after dark.
A week of storms batters Hais: 1 roof torn away.
